hypothesis: If Thompson is right, the constant (equiangular) spiral angle computed from measured whorl expansion in gastropod shells is almost never below 80° and mostly lies between 80° and 85°.
pass_criterion: Converting each shell's whorl expansion rate W (ratio of successive whorl radii per 360° turn) to the spiral angle alpha = arctan(2π / ln W), then taking the sample of specimens: at least 90% have alpha >= 80°, and at least 60% fall within 80°-85°. For the Nautilus-like case, specimens with W near 3 must give a median alpha within 80° ± 2°.
fail_criterion: Fewer than 90% of specimens have alpha >= 80°, or fewer than 60% fall within 80°-85°, or the median alpha for specimens with W between 2.5 and 3.5 lies outside 78°-82°.
interpretation: Thompson's constant angle is the angle between the tangent and the radius vector of a logarithmic spiral. For a whorl expansion W per turn, tan(alpha) = 2π/ln W, so W = 3 gives alpha ≈ 80°. This is computed from the dataset's whorl expansion parameters (e.g., the hangle output table of fitted helicospiral parameters), applied to the planispiral/projected component of each shell. The dataset's authors report that the logarithmic helicospiral assumptions fail in all 25 species studied, so specimen-level fits are approximate and the test measures the angle implied by the fitted expansion rate. Gastropod shells are helicospiral, not planar, so the projected spiral is used; the test is limited to the planar coiling component. Ammonoids and Nautilus are not in this dataset, so only the gastropod part of the claim is tested.

dataset.publisher: Dryad (Collins, Klapaukh, Crampton, Gazley, Schipper, Maksimenko, Hines)

It covers the gastropod part of the claim only.
